281.title: Not knowing where I'm going
281.hook: his best-known prayer admits he doesn't know the road, but trusts the desire to please God pleases God
281.howItsDone: Some Catholics pray Merton's prayer from Thoughts in Solitude in times of discernment, and it appears on prayer cards and at retreats.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fourth and Walnut, Transfiguration: a street corner where Merton saw strangers shining. Your line was they were shining. Today, a short prayer he wrote about not knowing.

So, what's the plan? The question shows up after graduation. After the divorce. After the diagnosis, the layoff, the move. Sometimes there isn't one, and a confident answer at the family dinner covers the gap until the lights go out. Thomas Merton, a famous monk, a man people wrote to for spiritual advice, put on paper for anyone to read that he didn't know where he was going. That's the opening of a prayer he's remembered for.
screen: `SO, WHAT'S THE PLAN?` → `A CONFIDENT ANSWER, NO PLAN.` → `HE DOESN'T KNOW WHERE HE'S GOING.`

segments.voice: First, where it's from. The prayer sits in a small book called Thoughts in Solitude, published in 1958. It's short, a single paragraph. Second, what it admits. Merton tells God, in his own words, that he doesn't see the road ahead or know where it ends. He goes further: he doesn't really know himself, and thinking he's following God's will doesn't mean he actually is. That's a startling thing for a monk to say. No false certainty at all. Third, the turn. Then comes the line people hold onto. Merton says he believes that the desire to please God does in fact please God. He hopes he has that desire in everything he does, and he trusts that if he keeps it, God will lead him by the right road, even when he can't tell. The desire counts, even when the map is missing. Fourth, the old roots. Scripture has people who set out without a map. The Letter to the Hebrews says of Abraham, in the Douay-Rheims: "he went out, not knowing whither he went." And the psalm says: "Thy word is a lamp to my feet." A lamp, not a floodlight. It lights the next step, not the whole road. Merton isn't praising confusion. He's saying faith can be honest: in his prayer, not knowing is allowed, as long as the wanting stays.

segments.voice: Name one place in your life where you don't know the way, a decision, a relationship, a worry about what's next, and don't solve it; just admit it, quietly: I don't know. Then notice whether, under the worry, there's a wanting: to do the right thing, to be good, to be close to God. If you pray, you can bring God both, the not-knowing and the wanting, in your own words.

282.title: The hermitage (1965)
282.hook: he moves to a cinderblock house in the woods
282.carry: a small house in the woods

segments.voice: Yesterday: solitude, and trusting that the desire counts even without a map. Your line was the desire counts. Today, Merton's road leads into the woods.

Everybody has a daydream about a cabin. A little place at the end of a dirt road. No commute, no inbox, just trees and a porch and a kettle. For most people it stays a daydream. In August 1965, a fifty-year-old monk walked up a path through the Kentucky woods, about a mile from his abbey, to a plain cinderblock house with a fireplace and a porch. He'd been asking for this for years. Now he'd live there, mostly alone.
screen: `THE DAYDREAM ABOUT A CABIN.` → `A PATH THROUGH THE WOODS.` → `A CINDERBLOCK HOUSE, AUGUST 1965.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Hermit comes from the Greek eremos, the desert. The first Christian hermits went out into the deserts of Egypt and Syria in the third and fourth centuries, men and women like Saint Antony, looking for God in silence. Merton loved them, and translated some of their sayings in a small book, The Wisdom of the Desert. Second, the house. It had been put up around 1960 for meetings with visitors from other churches. Merton started spending afternoons there, then days, and in 1965 his abbot let him move in full time. He chopped wood, hauled water, prayed the psalms, read and wrote. He still walked down to the abbey most days for Mass and a meal. Third, why a hermit, if he was already a monk? Even a silent monastery is a busy place: schedules, jobs, hundreds of people, and by then Merton was famous and swamped with visitors. He wanted to go further into the solitude that had drawn him to Gethsemani in the first place. Fourth, the Gospel model. Jesus did this too. In Mark, in the Douay-Rheims: "And rising very early, going out, he went into a desert place: and there he prayed." A hermitage is that desert place, made permanent. And here's the surprise: Merton's hermitage years were some of his most connected. He wrote hundreds of letters from that porch, to poets, activists and religious teachers around the world. Solitude didn't shrink his world. It widened it.

283.title: The monk who spoke about war and race
283.hook: from the cloister he wrote letters against nuclear war and for civil rights
283.howItsDone: Catholic teaching on peace and human dignity runs through papal letters like Pacem in Terris (1963), and many Catholic peace and justice groups trace their inspiration in part to Merton's writing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hermitage: a cinderblock house where solitude widened Merton's world. Your line was a small house in the woods. Today, what came out of the quiet.

The early 1960s. Families are building fallout shelters in their backyards. Schoolkids practice hiding under their desks in case of a nuclear bomb. In the South, people marching for civil rights are being beaten on the evening news. And in a silent monastery in Kentucky, a monk is typing letter after letter to anyone who'll listen: this is wrong, and Christians should say so. Some people were grateful. Some were furious. Some told him monks should stay out of it.
screen: `FALLOUT SHELTERS AND DUCK-AND-COVER.` → `MARCHERS BEATEN ON THE NEWS.` → `A MONK TYPING LETTERS.`

segments.voice: First, war. In 1961 and 1962, Merton wrote what he called the Cold War Letters, to friends, scholars and activists, arguing that nuclear war could never be squared with the Gospel. When he tried to publish on the subject, his order's superior general told him to stop. Merton obeyed and didn't publish that book. But he kept writing to friends, and the letters were copied and passed from hand to hand. Second, the surprise. In 1963, Pope John XXIII issued Pacem in Terris, Peace on Earth, a letter to the whole world calling for an end to the arms race. Merton felt the Church had said out loud what he'd been told to keep quiet. Third, race. In essays collected in 1964, including one called Letters to a White Liberal, Merton wrote that racism was a sickness of the whole society, not just a Southern problem, and that white Christians had to listen to Black Americans rather than tell them to wait. Later that year he hosted a small retreat at Gethsemani for peace activists, to pray about what faith asked of them. Fourth, the root. Merton said this came from contemplation, not from politics. Years before, on a Louisville street corner, he had seen every stranger shining. You can't see that and then shrug at a bomb or a beating. Jesus said, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." And Paul: "you are all one in Christ Jesus." For Merton, silence wasn't the opposite of speaking up. It was where the words came from.

If you pray, you can pray for them first.

284.title: Friends across traditions
284.hook: he corresponded with Zen and Jewish teachers and hosted Thich Nhat Hanh
284.howItsDone: The Catholic Church has official offices for dialogue with other religions, and Catholic monks and nuns, through groups like Monastic Interreligious Dialogue, still meet with Buddhist and other monastics to pray and talk.

segments.voice: Yesterday, peacemakers: the monk who spoke about war and race from the quiet of the cloister. Your line was silence that speaks. Today, the friends that quiet made.

Two old friends in a diner booth. One prays, one doesn't. They vote differently. They've argued for years, and they still meet for coffee every month, and each leaves a little larger. Neither has to pretend to agree. Thomas Merton had friendships like that all over the world, in an age of airmail. A Zen scholar in Japan. A rabbi in New York. A young Vietnamese monk who walked up the road to Gethsemani.
screen: `TWO OLD FRIENDS IN A DINER BOOTH.` → `NOBODY HAD TO PRETEND.` → `FRIENDS ALL OVER THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: First, the letters. From the late 1950s on, Merton wrote to people across many faiths. He corresponded for years with D. T. Suzuki, the Japanese scholar who brought Zen Buddhism to many English readers, and flew to New York in 1964 to meet him. He wrote to Abraham Joshua Heschel, the Jewish teacher and theologian; to Louis Massignon, a Catholic scholar of Islam; and to Muslim scholars about Sufi prayer. Second, the visit. In May 1966, the Vietnamese Buddhist monk Thich Nhat Hanh came to Gethsemani while touring America to speak about the war in his country. The two monks talked for hours. Afterward Merton published a short piece called Nhat Hanh Is My Brother, asking Americans to listen to him. Third, the Church's own turn. In 1965 the Second Vatican Council issued a short declaration called Nostra Aetate, In Our Time. It says the Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions, and it calls Catholics to dialogue with respect. Merton had been living that, one letter at a time. Paul said it long before, in the Douay-Rheims: "But prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Fourth, without erasing. Merton never pretended all traditions were the same, and he never asked anyone to leave their own. He stayed a Catholic monk to the end; his friends stayed Buddhist, Jewish, Muslim. What they shared was honesty, prayer and real curiosity. Friendship didn't flatten the differences. It made room for them.

285.title: Solitude is not escape
285.hook: being alone is for love of others, not away from them
285.howItsDone: Catholic contemplative monks and nuns, like Trappists and Carmelites, live largely hidden lives, and the Church teaches that their prayer serves the whole world; many lay Catholics make a holy hour of silent prayer for others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, friends across traditions, Nostra Aetate: letters and visits that honored every difference. Your line was friendship without erasing. Today, how a hermit could have so many friends.

There are two ways to be alone in a room. One is loneliness: the phone that doesn't ring, the scroll through other people's lives, the sense of being left out. The other is different. Someone shuts the door on purpose. The house goes quiet. And somehow the people they love come closer, not further away. The first gets talked about all the time. The second hardly ever gets a name. Thomas Merton spent his last years alone in the woods, and he insisted he hadn't run away from anyone.
screen: `TWO WAYS TO BE ALONE.` → `LONELINESS ACHES.` → `SHUTTING THE DOOR ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Solitude comes from the Latin solus, alone. But in the Christian tradition, being alone was never the point. The desert hermits went out alone, and, the stories say, people came a long way to ask them for advice. Second, Merton's claim. Across his books, Merton kept saying it: a person doesn't go into solitude to get away from people, but to learn how to love them better. He warned that solitude chosen out of contempt for others, or to avoid them, is just loneliness with a nice name. Real solitude, he said, makes you more aware of your bond with everyone. The hermit discovers he's carrying the whole world with him. Third, Jesus's pattern. Luke says, in the Douay-Rheims: "And he retired into the desert, and prayed." Then he comes back, and the crowds are waiting. Before he chose his twelve apostles, Luke says, he spent the whole night alone on a mountain in prayer. Solitude first, then people. Solitude for the people. Fourth, the Catholic picture. Catholics believe prayer isn't private property. A monk in his cell, a grandmother with her rosary at midnight, a hermit in Kentucky: each prayer joins the prayer of the whole Church, and reaches people the one praying will never meet. The Second Vatican Council said communities given wholly to contemplation hold a distinguished place in the Church. Alone, but for everyone.
screen: `SOLUS — ALONE.` · `NOT AWAY FROM PEOPLE, BUT FOR THEM.` · `HE RETIRED INTO THE DESERT.` · `EVERY PRAYER JOINS THE WHOLE CHURCH.` · then, large: `ALONE, BUT FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes or lower them, and notice that you're by yourself in this moment. Then let three people come to mind, one at a time, holding each for a few breaths: someone you love, someone you find difficult, someone you've never met, a stranger in a hospital tonight, a kid somewhere scared. If you pray, pray for each of them; if you don't, just wish them well.

286.title: Polonnaruwa (1968)
286.hook: before the great stone Buddhas in Sri Lanka he describes a clarity he'd long sought
286.howItsDone: Catholic contemplatives speak of a simple, loving gaze in prayer, and many Catholics practice it by looking long at an icon, a crucifix, the Blessed Sacrament or creation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, solitude is not escape: being alone for love of others. Your line was alone, for them. Today, Merton's long journey takes him far from Kentucky.

Autumn 1968. After twenty-seven years as a monk, Thomas Merton is given leave for a long journey abroad. He flies to Asia: Bangkok, then India, up into the Himalayan foothills, where he meets the Dalai Lama three times and they talk about prayer and meditation. Then, in early December, Sri Lanka, and an ancient ruined city called Polonnaruwa, where huge figures of the Buddha are carved straight into a wall of granite. He takes off his shoes and walks up to them across the wet grass. And something happens there that, he'll write, makes his whole Asian journey come clear.
screen: `AUTUMN 1968: ASIA.` → `THE DALAI LAMA, THREE TIMES.` → `BAREFOOT BEFORE THE STONE.`

segments.voice: First, the place. Polonnaruwa was a royal capital of Sri Lanka about nine hundred years ago. At a site called Gal Vihara, craftsmen cut enormous figures out of a single granite outcrop: the Buddha seated in meditation, a tall standing figure, and the Buddha lying on his side, at peace. They're still there, weathered, calm, open to the sky. Second, what Merton saw. In his journal, published after his death as The Asian Journal, he wrote that, looking at those faces, he was suddenly jerked out of his habitual way of seeing. Everything became clear, obvious and simple: the rock, the figures, the sky. He felt he'd seen what he'd been obscurely looking for all his life. Third, what it wasn't. Merton didn't become a Buddhist. He was a Catholic monk on that grass, and he died one, just over a week later. He was grateful to the Buddhist tradition for the beauty and stillness of that place, and received the moment as a gift. Buddhists and Catholics would each describe that clarity in their own words, and it's worth not blurring them. Fourth, the Catholic thread. Scripture talks about seeing, too. Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God." And Paul: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face." For Merton, Polonnaruwa was a glimpse through the glass: a moment of clean-hearted seeing, the kind contemplation had been preparing him for since that first mosaic in Rome.

287.title: Bangkok, 10 December 1968
287.hook: he died in an accident, twenty-seven years to the day after entering the monastery
287.howItsDone: Catholics pray for the dead at every Mass and especially in November, and when someone dies suddenly, families often ask a priest to offer a Mass for them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Polonnaruwa: barefoot before the great stone figures, a moment of clear seeing. Your line was seeing clearly. About a week later, Merton was in Bangkok.

Some dates line up in a way nobody could plan. On December 10, 1941, a young man rang the bell at the gate of Gethsemani and asked to become a monk. On December 10, 1968, that same man, now fifty-three and famous, gave a morning talk to a gathering of monks and nuns near Bangkok, went back to his room after lunch, and never came out. Twenty-seven years to the day. Today is gentle, about an ending.
screen: `DECEMBER 10, 1941: THE GATE.` → `DECEMBER 10, 1968: BANGKOK.` → `TWENTY-SEVEN YEARS TO THE DAY.`

segments.voice: First, the conference. Merton had come to Asia partly to speak at a meeting of Catholic monks and nuns from across the continent, at a retreat center outside Bangkok. That morning he gave his talk, on monastic life and the modern world. At the end he said they'd take questions later and, lightly, that for now he'd disappear. Second, the accident. After lunch he went to rest. He had taken a shower, and later that afternoon he was found dead, a faulty electric fan fallen across him. The most accepted account is that he was electrocuted. Some questions about the details have been raised since, and the sources don't settle all of them. Third, the journey home. His body was flown back to the United States on a military plane, alongside the bodies of American soldiers killed in Vietnam. The monk who had written so much against war went home with its dead. He was buried at Gethsemani, in the monks' cemetery, under a plain white cross like his brothers. Fourth, the day he began. Catholics don't treat a sudden death as meaningless or as punishment. Jesus said, in the Douay-Rheims: "Watch ye therefore, because you know not the day nor the hour." Not a threat, but an invitation to live each day awake. And the Church prays for those who die suddenly, trusting the words at every Catholic funeral: "I am the resurrection and the life." Merton's end came on the anniversary of his beginning.
